source_text: Well I think Rob's instructions are possibly contradictory in the current setting. "Do not start from scratch" means read the Lean code, it doesn't mean, "don't use the Lean elaborator".

fragments.text: Well I think Rob's instructions are possibly contradictory in the current setting.
"Do not start from scratch" means read the Lean code, it doesn't mean, "don't use the Lean elaborator".

reply_text:
㊥ ("possibly contradictory") I agree that gate 1 doesn't forbid the elaborator. Gate 1 is about not replacing mfuton's own pieces (parser, AST, catamorphism, extractor, emitter) with a parallel implementation, and Lean's elaborator is none of those. Two other rules don't fit your reading as neatly, though: gate 7 ("consumes the parsed Lean syntax tree") and "No second compiler". The test on two or three rows doesn't depend on settling that, so I'd go ahead with it now. Shall I?

㊟ ("doesn't mean, don't use the Lean elaborator") Here is where I think the contradiction you sense comes from. The C-authority rule from 2026-08-24 makes Lean's behaviour the authority and says to port its semantic logic. The Operator Direction asks for a small generic compiler. Both assumed the needed Lean subset was small. The census shows the subset is most of Lean's term elaborator. Under that finding, obeying gate 7 means rebuilding Lean's elaborator in Python, and that rebuild is the "second compiler" and the declaration-by-declaration convergence the mission forbids. Once the facts changed, the gates can't all be met together.

㊭ (how to resolve it) You could read the elaborated term as part of the frontend. mfuton already runs Lean natively to parse (LeanPy), so asking the same library to elaborate extends the existing frontend rather than replacing it. The catamorphism and module emitter would then take Lean's output instead of raw syntax. That fits gates 1 and 2 and the "small generic compiler" aim. Gate 7 would need an amendment to name elaborated terms as an allowed input. I'd write that amendment once the test shows the route works, so Rob sees a result before being asked about a rule.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I dispatch the test (Lean's compiled output for two or three failing rows → a throwaway translator → checked against the preregistered expected output, outside mfuton-share), with a bell back to me?

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.text: ("the lean elaborator says exactly what to do") You're right, and the route was never actually taken. What got adopted was a weaker form: Lean is used as an answer key (preregistered expected output per row) and as a curriculum (claude-3's census of which elaborator features each row uses). The port still has to rebuild each elaborator step in its own Python, one 30–60 minute probe at a time, and that rebuilding is the detail the agents are lost in. The full route, where Lean elaborates and the port only translates Lean's output to Python, is ruled out by Rob's mission gates. I'd suggest first testing it on one row outside the repo; the question at the end is whether to do that.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.text: (why the strong form wasn't taken) The mission (`M-lean-subset-python-compiler-for-generated-parser-combinators.md`) rules it out in three places. Gate 1 says "DO NOT START FROM SCRATCH". Gate 7 says the compiler consumes "the parsed Lean syntax tree". Scope Out says "No second compiler". A compiler that takes Lean's elaborated term as input would replace the port's front end, so the queue took the form those rules allow. That form tells agents what the right answer is, but not how to get there from source syntax.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
claude-6
previous_reply_acts.text: (why the strong form would be a short plan) It's closer than it sounds. The port already loads Lean's native library to parse (361 s of native calls in the cold profile), and the elaborator is in that same library. codex-6 is already capturing Lean's compiler output per row (`compiled.txt`, the mono stage), but only for checking answers. That intermediate language has a handful of constructs (let, fun, join points, cases, return), so a translator from it to Python would be the "relatively small generic compiler" the mission's own Operator Direction asks for. That section also says "not gradual declaration-by-declaration convergence", which is what the current route is turning into. So the strong route fits the mission's stated aim and breaks its gates.
